🎮 PINBALL MACHINE DIY – EPISODE 5: THE PLAYFIELD COMES TO LIFE!
In this fifth episode of the Pinball Machine project, we finally dive into the core of the new table — a completely redesigned build featuring colored playfields that give the flipper a truly professional and eye-catching look. Every section of the surface has been carefully planned, with new lighting points, transparent inserts, and dedicated areas for all the mechanical components.

🔧 Upgraded Ball Counting System
One of the biggest improvements in this episode is the new ball counting mechanism. A combination of sensors and levers now allows the system to detect only one ball at a time, automatically blocking the previous one to prevent errors. It’s a major upgrade in reliability and precision — a custom-designed solution built entirely from scratch.

💥 New Ball Launcher with Return Chimneys
The ball launcher gets a full redesign too, now featuring custom “chimneys” that guide the ball back perfectly onto the playfield. The system blends power and precision, using a combination of metal parts and 3D-printed components for a strong yet refined mechanism.

🧩 Assembling the Second Half of the Machine
This stage covers the full assembly of the second section of the pinball, including flippers, bumpers, sensors, and lighting. It’s the moment when the project truly starts to look like a real arcade machine — every component finally comes together and the playfield starts to take shape.

🏆 Custom Score Targets
Finally, I design and produce the custom score targets — small pieces of functional art that combine design and purpose, essential for the scoring system and for giving the flipper that authentic, professional arcade feel.

💡 A packed episode full of upgrades, testing, and clever engineering that brings me one step closer to the final goal: building a fully working pinball machine entirely from scratch!

The Cutting Room Floor is a site dedicated to unearthing and researching unused and cut content from video games. From debug menus, to unused music, graphics, enemies, or levels, many games have content never meant to be seen by anybody but the developers — or even meant for everybody, but cut due to time/budget constraints.

Feel free to browse our collection of games and start reading. Up for research? Try looking at some stubs and see if you can help us out. Just have some faint memory of some unused menu/level you saw years ago but can't remember how to access it? Feel free to start a page with what you saw and we'll take a look. If you want to help keep this site running and help further research into games, feel free to donate.

text.text: 52-year-old data tape could contain only known copy of UNIX V4
It might have the first-ever version of UNIX written in C

A 52-year-old data tape discovered at the University of Utah may contain the only known copy of UNIX Fourth Edition. If verified, it could hold the first version of UNIX written in the C programming language. The tape is being sent to the Computer History Museum for recovery, with software librarian Al Kossow leading the effort to extract its contents.

A tape-based piece of unique Unix history may have been lying quietly in storage at the University of Utah for 50+ years. The question is whether researchers will be able to take this piece of middle-aged media and rewind it back to the 1970s to get the data off.

text.text: Legendary game designer, programmer, Space Invaders champion, and LGBTQ trailblazer Rebecca Heineman has died

texts.text: Game developer Rebecca Heineman has died after being diagnosed with cancer last month. The news was shared to Bluesky by Heineman's friend,
, while the most recent post on

is a goodbye message stating that her health was rapidly deteriorating, and she was entering palliative care. Heineman was 62, and the GoFundMe will remain live to help her family make final arrangements.

Born in 1963, Heineman initially made a mark on the industry by winning a national Space Invaders tournament in 1980 in New York, becoming the first formally recognized US champion of any videogame. She went on to have a far-reaching career, being credited on 67 games according to

text.text: Heineman co-founded Interplay in 1983 alongside Brian Fargo, Jay Patel, and Troy Worrell. The developer and publisher was the source of many foundational PC games, including Wasteland, Fallout, and Baldur's Gate. Heineman designed and programmed a number of games at Interplay, with her most prominent design credit being The Bard's Tale 3: Thief of Fate.

texts.text: Heineman's friend and colleague from Interplay, Brian Fargo, shared a

on X. "Rebecca Heineman sadly passed away," Fargo wrote. "Known her since the 80s when I'd drive her to work, one of the most brilliant programmers around. A real gut punch earlier today when she messaged me: 'We have gone on so many adventures together! But, into the great unknown! I go first!!!'"

Later, in the '90s and 2000s, Heineman made a name primarily as a programmer, particularly on ports like the Macintosh versions of Wolfenstein 3D, Baldur's Gate, and Icewind Dale. The saga of Heineman overcoming a deranged businessman to solo program the ill-fated 3DO port of Doom in mere weeks has become a bit of an internet legend: Here's
and
recounting the tale.
Heineman publicly came out as transgender in the 2000s, and was married to fellow games industry legend Jennell Jaquays. Heineman was the recipient of Gayming's
, with the site writing that "her advocacy for LGBTQ+ inclusion, accessibility, and diversity in tech has inspired countless developers and players."
Jaquays died of complications from Guillain–Barré syndrome in January 2024, and Heineman was blindsided last month by an
. She turned to GoFundMe to help with the costs of treatment, where fans, friends, and industry peers showed up to support the developer.

webpage.title: Improved layout for Technics KN5000 by felipesanches · Pull Request #14558 · mamedev/mame

raw.message: https://github.com/mamedev/mame/pull/14558

After a month-long side-quest dedicated to implementing the layouts for the Access Virus synths, I'm now back to the Technics KN5000 main-quest 😉
So I've use my gained XP in crafting fine layouts to improve the KN5000 one.
It used to be dark and ugly, focusing on being merely functional, while the external artwork provided the nice colors and the button shapes.
For reference, here is what the external artwork looks like

But now (via PR #14558) most of that is available in the internal layout. I think the only thing missing are the gradients because the svg renderer in MAME does not support that yet. 
I was very careful to make smart use of hand-crafted SVG snippets for describing each kind of button shape and then reuse it across the layout, so it is not a big wall of floats, but instead a carefully optimized file. 
It also now contains 2 views:
The "compact" one
And the "Screen close-up" one

webpage.description:
I've added PIO support to One ROM Fire - and not just any PIO support, but a completely autonomous PIO+DMA chain that is over twice as performant as the existing CPU-based algorithm.

This is a deep dive into how I use the PIOs and DMA together on the RP2350 for maximum performance, beating any other algorithm I've seen for ROM serving on microcontrollers.

I also show off an anomoly that I can't explain in one of my VIC-II video chips, exposed by this algorithm.

🔗 **Links**

One ROM website: https://onerom.org/
